chapter: Vanguard and the Spirituals to Swing reissue
title: Taking Vanguard, Dolly bluegrass albums, finding the Spirituals to Swing tapes
summary: Dolly encouraged him to take Vanguard; after Sugar Hill was bought they made The Grass Is Blue and Little Sparrow. In the vault he found the Spirituals to Swing tapes.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: great artist, no matter what, even the political backlash in the 50s, it was Vanguard. I said I’d do the same thing the Solomon Brothers do. Just find great artists no matter what the genre and make it an artist-friendly label. And he called me and he called me and picked my brain. And I remember getting off the phone one day and I remember telling my assistant then, Jenny, I said, “I think he’s going to offer me a job.” And she said, “What would you do?” I said, “I would take it and you would do it with me. You’d still be my assistant.” And I went up to L.A. on one of the trips and went to Santa Monica, and he did offer me the position. And by that time I had told Dolly that Larry Welk’s offered me this job to do Vanguard. And I said it’s like — it would open up a whole new arena for me of different types of music. Signing new artists. And she said, “Jump on it. Do it.” Dolly said that to me. And then she stayed on Universal. And so I went to Vanguard, based in Santa Monica. I was back and forth once a month, to the point I had a condo in Santa Monica. I was there once a month. And right after I got there we bought Sugar Hill Records in Durham, North Carolina, which was primarily a bluegrass label. Doc Watson and Doyle Lawson and Quicksilver, and groups like that. And June of 1999 I get on a plane to go to L.A., sit down, and who walks in and gets in the seat right in front, Dolly. We just happened to get on the same plane. And I tapped her shoulder and she flipped out and made whoever was sitting next to her to change seats with me. So we sat together on the way to L.A. It was June of ’99. And I said during the conversation I said, “We bought this label in Durham, North Carolina. Sugar Hill Records. Bluegrass, this and that. I said, “Would you ever consider doing a bluegrass record?” So we started talking about it on that flight and went to dinner that night in L.A. and put the whole idea together. And she said, “I’ve got to do a movie the rest of this month, and July, I’m open August.” So I said, “I’ll put it together.” And we got the best musicians, bluegrass musicians. She called it God’s Bluegrass Band. And we went in, in a day and a half and we cut the album. “The Grass is Blue” which won the Grammy, best bluegrass album; won the IBMA Bluegrass Music Association best bluegrass album. And then so now she was signed to Sugar Hill. Unbelievable. I had Vanguard and Sugar Hill. So things are going full circle. And the following year we did the follow-up, “Little Sparrow” won the Grammy. And like I said, we’re still friends to this day. So it all came around. But while I was at Vanguard, started at Vanguard, I was wandering around in the vaults one day. And I knew they had done the “Spirituals to Swing,” the old 33-1/3 LP. But I got to looking in the vault and I came across a whole shelf STS, STS. And I pull it out and it’s “Spirituals to Swing.” And I got chills. I get chills now thinking about it. It was originally recorded on disk when John Hammond did the concerts in 1938 and ’39 at Carnegie Hall. So it was recorded on disk.
